_about: answer = index of the right option (shuffled on screen); evidence = supporting sentence, review only; hint = gentle "look again" line.

printing-shop.q: What bold project did Franklin begin?
printing-shop.evidence: It was about this time I conceived the bold and arduous project of arriving at moral perfection.
printing-shop.hint: Look again at the very first line.

printing-shop.q: Why was it harder than he expected?
options: While he guarded against one fault, another surprised him
He had no time at all
printing-shop.evidence: While my care was employed in guarding against one fault, I was often surprised by another; habit took the advantage of inattention; inclination was sometimes too strong for reason.
printing-shop.hint: Look again at what went wrong.

printing-shop.q: Franklin says good habits must be “acquired and established”. What does he mean?
options: Knowing what is right is not enough — you have to practise it
printing-shop.evidence: and that the contrary habits must be broken, and good ones acquired and established, before we can have any dependence on a steady, uniform rectitude of conduct.
printing-shop.hint: Look again at what he concluded.

virtues.q: How long did Franklin give to each virtue?
virtues.evidence: I determined to give a week’s strict attention to each of the virtues successively.

virtues.q: Why did he put Temperance first?
options: It gives a cool, clear head for the rest
It was the easiest to spell
virtues.evidence: Temperance first, as it tends to procure that coolness and clearness of head, which is so necessary where constant vigilance was to be kept up
virtues.hint: Look again at his reasons for the order.

virtues.q: Franklin compares his plan to weeding a garden one bed at a time. Why?
options: Trying to fix everything at once is too much
virtues.evidence: And like him who, having a garden to weed, does not attempt to eradicate all the bad herbs at once, which would exceed his reach and his strength, but works on one of the beds at a time

little-book.q: Which virtue gave Franklin the most trouble?
little-book.evidence: My scheme of _Order_ gave me the most trouble
little-book.hint: Look again at what he found hardest.

little-book.q: Why did Franklin add Humility to his list?
options: A Quaker friend told him he was thought proud
He had run out of ideas
little-book.evidence: My list of virtues contained at first but twelve; but a Quaker friend having kindly informed me that I was generally thought proud
little-book.hint: Look again at the thirteenth virtue.

little-book.q: The man said, “I think I like a speckled ax best.” What is Franklin warning about?
options: Giving up and pretending your faults don’t matter
little-book.evidence: have given up the struggle, and concluded that “a speckled ax was best”
little-book.hint: Look again at the story of the smith.

vault.q: What did Franklin mark in his little book for every fault?
vault.evidence: I might mark, by a little black spot, every fault I found upon examination to have been committed respecting that virtue upon that day.
vault.hint: Think about the pages of the little book.

vault.q: What question did Franklin ask himself each morning?
options: What good shall I do this day?
vault.evidence: What good shall I do this day?

vault.q: How long was one complete course through all the virtues?
vault.evidence: Proceeding thus to the last, I could go through a course complete in thirteen weeks, and four courses in a year.
vault.hint: Think about one virtue a week.

options: No — but he became a better and a happier man
He gave up after a week
vault.evidence: But, on the whole, though I never arrived at the perfection I had been so ambitious of obtaining, but fell far short of it, yet I was, by the endeavour, a better and a happier man than I otherwise should have been if I had not attempted it

vault.q: Why does Franklin say he might be “proud of my humility”?
options: Pride is so hard to beat it sneaks back in
vault.evidence: In reality, there is, perhaps, no one of our natural passions so hard to subdue as _pride_.

vault.q: What did Franklin always carry with him, even abroad?
vault.evidence: but I always carried my little book with me.
